slides.0.subtitle: Blind-tasting clues for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling
slides.1.title: Blind-tasting clues (general guidance)
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Grüner Veltliner
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Often white pepper, lime, green fruit and herbal notes; medium to high acidity; Smaragd-level wines are richer
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Riesling
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Often citrus, peach and minerality; high acidity; Wachau gneiss wines tend to be tight
slides.1.highlights.2.title: A caution
slides.1.highlights.2.content: These are tendencies, not rules; a blind conclusion must combine acidity, alcohol, aroma and structure, never one clue alone
slides.1.content: This page is general tasting guidance, not regulatory fact, and is not in the quiz.
slides.2.title: An MW-style essay template
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Define the question
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Open by answering the key words of the question and setting scope and position
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Three arguments
slides.2.highlights.1.content: For each argument: claim → fact (with year and number) → cause → what it means for the industry
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Counter-view and limits
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Acknowledge limits such as data years or source differences
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Conclusion
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Return to the question and give a reasoned judgement
slides.2.content: Sample question: "Discuss the impact of the DAC system on Austrian quality and branding."
slides.3.title: Short-answer practice: question and marking points
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Question 1
slides.3.highlights.0.content: “Explain how Wachau’s climate and topography affect the style and price of Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.” (about 250 words)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Marking points for question 1
slides.3.highlights.1.content: ① warm and cool air meet → diurnal range → acidity kept; ② Riesling on terrace gneiss, Grüner on lower loess; ③ thin soils, low rain → irrigation; ④ hand-worked terraces → high cost → premium Smaragd/Ried; ⑤ acknowledge limits (vintage variation, warming raises alcohol). Each point needs a cause and effect, not just a fact
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Question 2
slides.3.highlights.2.content: “Assess the impact of the DAC system on the quality and marketing of Austrian wine.” (about 350 words)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Marking points for question 2
slides.3.highlights.3.content: ① background: the turn to quality after 1985, Weinviertel the first DAC in 2002; ② strengths: style written into law (no oak or botrytis in Weinviertel), origin pyramid (Gebiets/Orts/Riedenwein) builds recognition; ③ limits: rules differ by DAC and are hard for consumers, and in the Wachau the Vinea Wachau marks coexist with the DAC; ④ the conclusion must take a view, e.g. “branding has worked, but communication costs remain high”
slides.3.content: Write your answer first, then check the points: each missing cause and effect costs a mark.
What structure is suggested for each argument in an MW essay?
B. Claim → fact → cause → industry meaning
C. Conclusion first with no explanation
An argument needs a claim, evidence, cause and meaning.
Why should a blind-tasting conclusion not rest on one clue?
A. Clues are tendencies and must be combined with acidity, alcohol, aroma and structure
B. Because the rules say so
C. Because there is only one wine
D. Because no reasoning is needed
Acknowledging "data years or source differences" belongs to which step?
That belongs to counter-view and limits.
